samasa.literal: he from whom fear has gone

morph.note: Nominative plural of उत्पत्ति. As object of श्रुत्वा the accusative उत्पत्तीः would be expected; the nominative is an epic (ārṣa) looseness, or the phrase is an anacoluthon (‘and the auspicious manifestations —’). The sense is not in doubt.
Present of √जन् (divādi, with the root shortened to जा- before य): literally ‘is born’, here with a predicate adjective, ‘becomes (fearless)’.
Nominative singular of the irregular stem पुंस् ‘man’ (strong stem पुमांस्-); genitive plural पुंसाम् in 12.15.

mantras.anvaya: मम एतत् माहात्म्यं तथा च (मम) शुभाः उत्पत्तयः युद्धेषु (मम) पराक्रमं च श्रुत्वा पुमान् निर्भयः जायते।
mantras.anvaya_en: An absolutive with three objects (माहात्म्यम्, उत्पत्तयः, पराक्रमम्) and a main clause with subject पुमान्, verb जायते and predicate निर्भयः.
mantras.lit: Having heard this Māhātmya of mine, and likewise the auspicious manifestations, and (my) valour in battles, a man becomes fearless.
mantras.tr: One who hears this account of my glory — my auspicious manifestations and my valour in battle — becomes free of fear.
mantras.tr_note: The readable translation takes the manifestations and the valour as the content of the Māhātmya, which is what the text is; the Sanskrit lists them side by side with तथा च.

comm.t: Three things heard — the Māhātmya, the Devī’s auspicious manifestations (उत्पत्तयः) and her valour in battle — make the hearer fearless. The manifestations are her appearances in the text: from the gods’ tejas (chapter 2), from the body of Pārvatī (chapter 5), and the forms foretold in 11.41–55.
The tradition connects the fruit with the content: one who has heard how the Goddess overcame every enemy in battle shares in her fearlessness.

flags.uncertain: उत्पत्तयः शुभाः is nominative where the accusative is expected after श्रुत्वा; it is construed as a second object (an ārṣa looseness). The Gita Press reading is kept.

sandhi.note: Before s the visarga may become s (रिपवस्संक्षयम्) or, as is usual in print, stay visarga.
Final m before c becomes anusvāra; च + उप… → चोप… (a + u → o).
Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra; so also पुंसां माहात्म्यं मम.

morph.note: √नन्द् is parasmaipada in classical usage (नन्दति); the ātmanepada नन्दते is an epic (ārṣa) form, common in Purāṇic verse, with no difference of meaning.
Genitive plural of the present participle शृण्वत् (stem शृणु- with u → v before the vowel ending): ‘of (men) hearing’.
Present of √या ‘to go’ with an abstract noun in the accusative, a common idiom: संक्षयं यान्ति ‘go to destruction, perish’.

mantras.anvaya: मम माहात्म्यं शृण्वतां पुंसां रिपवः संक्षयं यान्ति, कल्याणं च उपपद्यते, कुलं च नन्दते।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three coordinate clauses with different subjects (रिपवः, कल्याणम्, कुलम्); the genitive phrase पुंसां … शृण्वताम् (‘of men who hear’) belongs to all three.
mantras.lit: Enemies go to destruction, welfare comes about, and the family rejoices — of men who hear my Māhātmya.
mantras.tr: For those who hear my glory, enemies perish, good fortune comes, and their family flourishes.
mantras.tr_note: The genitive पुंसां शृण्वताम् is grammatically attached to कुलम्; the readable translation lets it govern all three clauses, as the sense requires.

comm.t: Three further fruits for those who hear the text: the destruction of enemies, the arrival of welfare, and the flourishing of the family.

A modern reading may take the ‘enemies’ (रिपवः) inwardly as well, as the passions Indian thought calls the six inner enemies (षड्रिपु). The verse itself speaks of outward enemies, beside welfare and family.

samasa.sense: a propitiatory rite performed to avert harm

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (दुःस्वप्न is a prādi tatpuruṣa: दुष्टः स्वप्नः)
samasa.literal: in the seeing of a bad dream

samasa.alt: Also readable as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, ग्रहाणां पीडाः ‘the planets’ afflictions’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Optative of √श्रु (stem शृणु- + याः + त्): ‘one should hear’ — the optative of prescription.
Locative singular of the n-stem कर्मन् (कर्मणि, with ṇ after r).

mantras.anvaya: सर्वत्र शान्तिकर्मणि तथा दुःस्वप्नदर्शने उग्रासु ग्रहपीडासु च मम माहात्म्यं शृणुयात्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three locatives of occasion and one prescriptive optative, with an unexpressed generic subject (‘one’).
mantras.lit: In every rite of pacification, likewise on seeing a bad dream, and in severe afflictions from the planets, one should hear my Māhātmya.
mantras.tr: At every rite for averting harm, after an evil dream, and when the planets afflict severely, let my glory be heard.
mantras.tr_note: The optative ‘one should hear’ is rendered as an impersonal ‘let … be heard’.

comm.t: The Devī prescribes her Māhātmya for three occasions of śānti (averting harm): propitiatory rites in general, bad dreams, and planetary afflictions. The next verse gives the result for each.
On this verse the tradition prescribes the Saptaśatī pāṭha as a remedy in the rites of pacification connected with dreams and planets, in place of or alongside other propitiatory rites.

morph.note: उप + √जन्, present: ‘arises, comes to be’; with the predicate सुस्वप्नम् it means ‘turns into a good dream’.
Instrumental plural of the r-stem नृ ‘man’ (नृ + भिस्); agent of the participle दृष्टम्.
स्वप्न is masculine; the neuter here (with दृष्टम्, सुस्वप्नम्) treats ‘a bad dream’ as a thing seen. Epic usage allows this; the meaning is unaffected.

mantras.anvaya: उपसर्गाः दारुणाः ग्रहपीडाः च शमं यान्ति; नृभिः दृष्टं दुःस्वप्नं च सुस्वप्नम् उपजायते।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: the first with two subjects and the idiom शमं यान्ति ‘come to rest’; the second with subject दुःस्वप्नम्, verb उपजायते and the predicate सुस्वप्नम्.
mantras.lit: Calamities go to rest, and the dreadful afflictions from the planets; and a bad dream seen by men becomes a good dream.
mantras.tr: Calamities are stilled, and the harsh afflictions of the planets; and the evil dream that men have seen turns into a good one.

comm.t: The result of the hearing prescribed in 12.16: calamities and planetary afflictions subside, and an evil dream is turned into a good one — its bad omen is reversed.
A modern reading: what was dreaded does not merely disappear; it is changed into its opposite. Fear met with the remembrance of grace can become a sign of protection.

flags.uncertain: दुःस्वप्नम् / सुस्वप्नम् are neuter here though स्वप्न is normally masculine; the forms are taken as epic usage, not as a corruption.
